📽 Slide 5 / 55 — Who is x, who is y

Opening (0:00–0:02) and why a line comes after r

Parking Lot from Class 6. The question asked most often during Brick 6 was: *"Why is std_dev(xs) == statistics.stdev(xs) False when both print 6.352?"* The two functions add the same numbers in a different order, and a computer stores most decimal numbers only approximately (IEEE 754 floating point). The last digit of the two results differs: 6.352072224780001 against 6.3520722247800006. The rule stays the one from Class 6: compare floats with math.isclose, never with ==.

Today's plan. Three parts of fifteen minutes, each followed by a five-minute activity: (1) correlation and simple linear regression, (2) the agent loop of JARVIS, (3) turning numbers into a decision, presenting the Alpha and giving feedback. The workshop that follows is the Alpha demo: five minutes per team, three minutes of feedback.

Where the line comes from. In Brick 4 you computed Pearson's correlation coefficient r with statistics.correlation and found r = +0.883 between interruptions and minutes for the stand-up notes routine. The coefficient r answers one question: how strongly, and in which direction, do two numeric variables move together along a straight line? It does not answer the owner's question: "How many minutes would we save per run with two interruptions fewer?" That question needs a number measured in minutes per interruption. That number is the slope of a straight line fitted to the data, and finding that line is the job of simple linear regression.

Two words fix the roles of the variables. The explanatory variable x is the variable used to explain or predict (here: interruptions during a run). The response variable y is the variable we want to explain or predict (here: minutes the run took). A scatter plot draws one point per run at position (x, y). Simple means one explanatory variable; linear means the model is a straight line, ŷ = a + b·x.

In Brick 7, StatsEngine receives two new methods written by you: correlation(xs, ys) and linear_regression(xs, ys). As in Class 6, the engine is yours and the statistics module is the oracle: a trusted implementation used only to check your results in tests.

📽 Slide 6 / 55 — Three totals carry every formula
📽 Slide 7 / 55 — Five lines: r, b, a, ŷ, R²
📽 Slide 8 / 55 — Least squares: residuals, SSE and two checks

Three totals carry every formula

Every formula of this lesson is built from deviations: the distance of each value from its mean, x − x̄ and y − ȳ. A deviation is negative below the mean and positive above it. From the deviations we compute three totals:

Sxx = Σ(x − x̄)² Syy = Σ(y − ȳ)² Sxy = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)
  • Sxx is never negative. It measures how spread out x is; Sxx = 0 means every x is the same.
  • Syy measures the spread of y in the same way.
  • Sxy can be positive or negative. A product (x − x̄)(y − ȳ) is positive when x and y are on the same side of their means, so a positive Sxy means that runs with more interruptions than average tend to take more minutes than average.

With the three totals, the whole lesson fits in five lines:

r = Sxy / √(Sxx · Syy)
b = Sxy / Sxx
a = ȳ − b · x̄
ŷ = a + b · x
R² = r² (one explanatory variable) = 1 − SSE / SST
  • r, the Pearson correlation coefficient, lies between −1 and +1. The course wording from Class 4: below 0.10 negligible, 0.10–0.29 weak, 0.30–0.69 moderate, 0.70 or more strong.
  • b, the slope, is the change in the predicted y for one more unit of x. Its unit is "unit of y per unit of x": minutes per interruption.
  • a, the intercept, is the predicted y when x = 0. The formula a = ȳ − b·x̄ forces the line through the point (x̄, ȳ).
  • ŷ ("y-hat") is the fitted value: the point of the line above a given x.
  • A residual is e = y − ŷ, the observed value minus the fitted value.
  • SSE (the sum of squared errors) is Σ(y − ŷ)², the sum of squared residuals; SST (the total sum of squares) is Syy, the variation of y around its mean.
  • R², the coefficient of determination, is the share of the variation of y that the line accounts for, between 0 and 1.

The method that produces b and a is called least squares (in full, ordinary least squares, OLS): among all straight lines, it picks the one with the smallest SSE. Two properties follow and are useful as checks: the line passes through (x̄, ȳ), and when the model has an intercept the residuals add up to exactly zero.

A form you will meet in videos and textbooks: b = r · s_y / s_x, where s_y and s_x are the sample standard deviations. It gives the same number, because the n − 1 in both standard deviations cancels.

Worked example by hand: five stand-up runs of S5

Staff member S5 wrote stand-up notes on five days with 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 interruptions. These are real rows of the teaching dataset, sorted by x:

Five stand-up runs of S5 (teaching dataset), with the columns of the hand calculation
dateinterruptions xminutes yx − x̄y − ȳ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)(x − x̄)²(y − ȳ)²
2026-09-2106-2-510425
2026-09-23110-1-1111
2026-09-2421100000
2026-09-1631413319
2026-09-3041423649
total105500Sxy = 20Sxx = 10Syy = 44

Means. Σx = 10 and Σy = 55, so x̄ = 10 / 5 = 2 and ȳ = 55 / 5 = 11.

Totals. Adding the last three columns: Sxy = 20, Sxx = 10 and Syy = 44.

Slope. b = Sxy / Sxx = 20 / 10 = 2.0 minutes per interruption. For S5, each additional interruption goes with two more minutes of note writing.

Intercept. a = ȳ − b·x̄ = 11 − 2 × 2 = 7.0 minutes: the predicted length of a run with no interruption. The fitted line is ŷ = 7 + 2x.

Correlation. r = 20 / √(10 × 44) = 20 / √440 = 20 / 20.976 = 0.9535, a strong positive relationship.

R². R² = 0.9535² = 0.9091. The same value from the residuals: the fitted values are 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15; the residuals are −1, +1, 0, +1 and −1; SSE = 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 4; R² = 1 − 4 / 44 = 0.909. The line accounts for about 91 % of the variation of these five runs.

Checks. The residuals add up to 0, as least squares requires. No other straight line gives these five points a sum of squared residuals smaller than 4.

📽 Slide 12 / 55 — Four guards and the oracle

The same calculation in StatsEngine: two passes and four guards

The program of this lesson, regression_engine.py, computes the three totals exactly as on the board, in two passes over the data:

  1. First pass — compute x̄ and ȳ with mean().
  2. Second pass — visit the pairs with zip(xs, ys), compute the two deviations and add dx·dx, dx·dy and dy·dy to three running totals.

linear_regression() and correlation() both call this sums() method, so the two passes are written once. The deviation form is chosen on purpose: it reads like the formula and is numerically more stable than shortcut formulas such as Σxy − n·x̄·ȳ, which subtract two large numbers.

A method that receives impossible input must refuse it with a clear message, not return a wrong number. The engine has four guards, each raising ValueError:

  • x and y have different lengths — every x needs exactly one y;
  • fewer than two pairs — one point does not determine a line;
  • Sxx = 0 — every x is equal, so the slope would divide by zero;
  • Sxx = 0 or Syy = 0 in correlation() — r is undefined for a constant variable.

The oracle. statistics.linear_regression(xs, ys) (Python 3.10 or later) returns the slope and the intercept as a named tuple with the fields slope and intercept; statistics.correlation(xs, ys) returns r. The program compares its own results with the oracle using math.isclose, because floats computed in a different order differ in the last digits. In Class 10 these comparisons become pytest tests.

One more rule from Class 6 applies: never sort xs or ys separately before fitting. Sorting one list breaks the pairing of each x with its own y.

What the real data say: six routines, one method

Running the same method on the manual runs of each routine gives this table (output of the engine, rounded):

Minutes on interruptions, manual runs of each routine (engine output, rounded)

standup_notes70+0.8832.2116.6600.779strong

Two observations matter for the owner.

  1. The slopes are similar — between about 1.0 and 2.3 minutes per interruption for every routine.
  2. The strength is not. R² goes from 0.78 for stand-up notes to 0.05 for e-mail triage. A stand-up run takes about ten minutes, so two extra minutes per interruption is a large part of its variation. An e-mail run takes about 35 minutes and varies for many other reasons: the Monday backlog, the volume of e-mail, the speed of each person. Interruptions account for less than 5 % of that variation.

With the course wording, r = 0.883 is strong and r = 0.215 is weak. The e-mail slope (1.42) is therefore an estimate with much more uncertainty than the stand-up slope (2.21), even though both are printed with three decimals.

📽 Slide 17 / 55 — What the line does not prove

Forecasting, and where a forecast must stop

The fitted stand-up line is ŷ = 6.660 + 2.211x. A forecast is the fitted value for a chosen x:

  • 3 interruptions → ŷ = 6.660 + 2.211 × 3 = 13.3 minutes;
  • 1 interruption → ŷ = 6.660 + 2.211 × 1 = 8.9 minutes;
  • two interruptions fewer → a change of 2 × b = −4.42 minutes per run.

At 100 stand-up runs a month (5 staff × 20 working days), 4.42 minutes per run would be about 7.4 hours, or about 206 $ at 28 $/h — if removing the interruptions caused the change.

Interpolation and extrapolation. The 70 manual runs contain 0 to 4 interruptions (only one run had 4). A forecast for an x inside that range is an interpolation. A forecast outside it — 8 interruptions, for example — is an extrapolation: the formula still produces a number (24.4 minutes), but no observation ever checked the line there. StatsEngine.predict() refuses such a request with a ValueError that states the observed range.

The intercept. Here a = 6.66 minutes has a practical meaning, because x = 0 is inside the data (15 stand-up runs had no interruption). In many datasets x = 0 lies far outside the observed values; then a is only a construction value of the line.

What the line does not prove.

  • Correlation is not causation. A confounding variable can drive both x and y: a busy Monday brings more interruptions and more to write. The line describes the 70 runs; it does not show that muting notifications would shorten them.
  • The sample is small and local. Fourteen working days and five people of one studio; another team, or another month, can give another slope.
  • Look at the residuals before trusting a straight line. If the residuals form a curve, or grow with x (a fan shape), a straight line is the wrong summary.

The honest sentence for the owner therefore reads: "Each extra interruption is associated with about 2.2 more minutes per stand-up run (r = 0.88, R² = 0.78, n = 70)." Lesson 7.3 shows how to turn it into a decision with a stated risk.

Key terms of Lesson 7.1
termmeaning
explanatory variable (x)The variable used to explain or predict another one; here, interruptions per run.
response variable (y)The variable we want to explain or predict; here, minutes per run.
deviationThe distance of a value from its mean, x − x̄; negative below the mean, positive above it.
Sxx, Syy, SxyThe sums of squared deviations of x and of y, and the sum of cross-products of the deviations.
Pearson correlation coefficient (r)Sxy / √(Sxx·Syy), between −1 and +1: strength and direction of a straight-line relationship.
simple linear regressionA model ŷ = a + b·x with one explanatory variable, fitted by least squares.
slope (b)Sxy / Sxx: the change in predicted y for one more unit of x (minutes per interruption).
intercept (a)ȳ − b·x̄: the predicted y when x = 0; meaningful only when x = 0 is inside the data.
fitted value (ŷ)The point of the line above a given x.
residual (e)y − ŷ, the observed minus the fitted value.
least squaresThe method that chooses a and b so that the sum of squared residuals (SSE (sum of squared errors)) is as small as possible.
coefficient of determination (R²)1 − SSE/SST (total sum of squares) = r² for one explanatory variable: the share of the variation of y that the line accounts for.
interpolation / extrapolationA forecast inside / outside the range of x values that were observed.
confounding variableA third variable that influences both x and y and can create a correlation without a direct cause.
oracleA trusted implementation (here the statistics module) used only to check your own code.

Real-life example 7.1

A focus window for stand-up notes

Task of the exampleEstimate how many minutes per stand-up run are associated with each interruption, how reliable the estimate is, and what two interruptions fewer would mean — without extrapolating beyond the data.How it relates to Lesson 7.1It applies every formula of Lesson 7.1 (Sxx, Sxy, Syy, r, b, a, R², forecast and its limits) to the real teaching dataset, with the statistics module as the oracle.

The owner of Boréal Studio is considering a simple rule: from 9:00 to 9:15 every notification is muted while stand-up notes are written. Before she changes the team's habits, she asks the JARVIS team two questions: how many minutes could this save, and how sure are you?

The team answers with three steps. First, it checks the method by hand on five runs of S5 (b = 2.0, a = 7.0, r = 0.95). Second, it fits the line on all 70 manual stand-up runs and, for contrast, on the 55 manual e-mail runs, and compares each result with the oracle. Third, it computes the forecasts for 3 and for 1 interruption, the difference between them, and shows that the engine refuses a forecast for 8 interruptions.

Execution steps (every executed step stays here)
    Variables at this step (yellow = changed)

    Visualization of the lesson concept
    Step-by-step explanation of the program
    1. Find the data. DATA is built from the location of the script with pathlib, so the program runs on any computer without editing a path.
    2. **mean() with a guard.** An empty list raises ValueError instead of dividing by zero.
    3. **sums() — two passes.** The first pass computes x̄ and ȳ; the second visits the pairs with zip() and accumulates dx·dx, dx·dy and dy·dy. Two guards stop lists of different lengths and fewer than two pairs.
    4. **linear_regression().** It calls sums(), refuses Sxx = 0, then computes slope = sxy / sxx and intercept = y_bar − slope · x_bar, and returns them in the same order as the oracle.
    5. **correlation() and r_squared().** r = Sxy / √(Sxx·Syy), refused when x or y is constant; R² = r·r.
    6. **predict() with a range guard.** It returns a + b·x only when x lies between the smallest and the largest observed x; otherwise it raises ValueError (extrapolation).
    7. **load_pairs().** It reads the CSV (comma-separated values) file with csv.DictReader and keeps the interruptions and minutes of one routine and one tool, converting the text to integers.
    8. **report().** It prints n, r, b, a and R² on one line and compares the three numbers with statistics.linear_regression and statistics.correlation through math.isclose.
    9. **Part 1 of main().** The five runs of S5 reproduce the hand example: x̄ = 2, ȳ = 11, Sxx = 10, Sxy = 20, Syy = 44, ŷ = 7 + 2x, r = 0.9535, R² = 0.9091, and the five residuals −1, +1, 0, +1, −1.
    10. Part 2. The real manual runs: stand-up notes give r = +0.883, b = 2.211, a = 6.660, R² = 0.779; e-mail triage gives r = +0.215, b = 1.423, a = 32.946, R² = 0.046. Both lines print oracle match: True.
    11. Part 3. The forecasts 13.3 and 8.9 minutes, their difference −4.42 minutes per run, and the refusal of x = 8 with the observed range 0..4.
    12. Use the player. Press Start, then Pause inside sums(): the Steps window shows each line already executed, the Variables panel shows dx, dy and the three totals, and the visualization marks the pair being added.

    📽 Slide 21 / 55 — 7.2 What an agent is in JARVIS
    What an agent is in JARVIS
    In this course an agent is a program that receives a request written in ordinary language, decides which action matches it, performs that action with a tool and records what happened. The IBM (International Business Machines) video of this lesson describes agents built around a large language model (LLM) that plans and calls tools; JARVIS version 0 runs the same loop with written rules instead of a model. The loop has five steps, and each step belongs to one class of the design you drew in Brick 5:
    

    📽 Slide 22 / 55 — The loop: five steps, five owners
    The agent loop of JARVIS: five steps, five owners (values of the first request)
    stepquestion it answersowner (class.method)example value
    1 requestWhat did the person type?Agent.handle(text)"log 25 min email_triage"
    2 intentWhat does it mean?OfflineProvider.parse(text)Intent("log_time", {"minutes": 25, "routine": "email_triage"})
    3 toolWhich action matches?self.tools.get(intent.name)LogTimeTool
    4 resultDo it, and what is the reply?LogTimeTool.run(args, store)"logged 25 min of email_triage (entry #1)"
    5 logWhat happened, for the record?Store.log_run(...)runs row: 09:00:00, log_time, log_time, offline, ok = 1
    

    Six words carry the lesson:
    

    • request — the text a person types, for example log 25 min email_triage;
    • intent — the structured meaning of the request: a name that selects a tool, plus the arguments the tool needs;
    • provider — the component that turns a request into an intent (OfflineProvider today, ApiProvider in Class 10);
    • tool — a small class that performs one action and returns a reply;
    • result — the reply text shown to the person;
    • runs log — the runs table, where JARVIS writes one row per request: its own dataset.
    📽 Slide 23 / 55 — The Intent dataclass
    The Intent dataclass
    An intent is data, so it is a dataclass — the tool you used for TimeEntry in Class 5:
    

    @dataclass(frozen=True)
class Intent:
    name: str
    args: dict = field(default_factory=dict)
    

    • frozen=True makes an Intent read-only after creation: no tool can change it by mistake while it travels through the loop.
    • field(default_factory=dict) gives every Intent its own new dictionary. Writing args: dict = {} is refused by the dataclasses module (ValueError: mutable default … use default_factory), because one dictionary would be shared by every Intent — the mutable-default trap of Class 5.
    

    Examples: Intent("log_time", {"minutes": 25, "routine": "email_triage"}), Intent("daily_report") (no arguments), Intent("unknown", {"text": "book a flight to Paris"}).
    📽 Slide 26 / 55 — The OfflineProvider pattern, piece by piece
    Regular expressions: the pieces you need
    A regular expression (regex) is a pattern that describes a set of strings. Python's re module compares a pattern with a text and, when they match, returns the parts the pattern captured. Five kinds of pieces are enough for JARVIS:
    

    📽 Slide 24 / 55 — Regular expressions: the pieces you need
    The regular-expression pieces used by the OfflineProvider
    kindpiecemeaningexample in JARVIS
    literallogthe letters l, o, g in this orderlog 25 min …
    character class\d  \w  \s  [a-z_]a digit; a letter, digit or underscore; a space or tab; one character of the set\d matches 2 and 5 in 25
    quantifier+  *  ?  {4}one or more; zero or more; optional; exactly four\d+ = 25; \s* allows 45min; \d{4} = 2026
    group( )  (?P<name> )  (?: )  a|bcapture; capture with a name; group without capture; alternatives(?P<minutes>\d+); (?:minutes|min)
    anchor / boundary^  $  \bstart of text; end of text; edge of a word^\s*log … \s*$ ; min\b
    flagre.IGNORECASEletters match in either caseLOG = log
    

    Patterns are written as raw strings, r"...", so that a backslash such as \d reaches the regex engine unchanged. re.compile() turns the pattern into an object once; pattern.match(text) tries it from the first character, pattern.search(text) anywhere, pattern.fullmatch(text) on the whole text. A successful call returns a match object; match.group("minutes") returns the captured text and match.groupdict() all named groups as a dictionary. A failed call returns None — which is why the provider tests if match: before reading a group.
    

    The first idea on the board is the pattern of the schedule, r"log\s+(\d+)\s*min\s+(\w+)". Tested on three phrasings of the same request it gives:
    

    📽 Slide 25 / 55 — First idea vs three phrasings
    First idea vs OfflineProvider on three phrasings (program output)
    phrasingfirst idea r"log\s+(\d+)\s*min\s+(\w+)"OfflineProvider
    log 30 min invoice_check('30', 'invoice_check')log_time {minutes: 30, routine: invoice_check}
    log 45min social_post('45', 'social_post')log_time {minutes: 45, routine: social_post}
    LOG 20 minutes of schedulingNonelog_time {minutes: 20, routine: scheduling}
    

    The third phrasing fails for three separate reasons: the capital letters of LOG, the word minutes (after min comes u, not a space) and the word of. The OfflineProvider pattern fixes all three:
    

    ^\s*log\s+(?P<minutes>\d+)\s*(?:minutes|minute|mins|min|m)\b\s+(?:of\s+)?(?P<routine>[a-z_\-]+)\s*$
    

    Read it from left to right: start of the text and optional spaces; the word log; at least one space; the named group minutes (one or more digits); optional spaces; one of five spellings of the unit, longest first, followed by a word boundary \b; at least one space; an optional of ; the named group routine (letters, underscores, hyphens); optional spaces; end of the text. The flag re.IGNORECASE makes LOG and log equal. The alternatives are listed from the longest to the shortest so that the intention is visible; with \b the engine would backtrack to the right alternative anyway, but without \b a pattern (?:m|min) would stop after the m.
    📽 Slide 27 / 55 — Three rules, a keyword table, the same answer every time
    The OfflineProvider: three rules, one keyword table, the same answer every time
    OfflineProvider.parse(text) tries its rules in a fixed order and returns the first intent that fits:
    

    1. the log pattern above → Intent("log_time", {"minutes": …, "routine": …});
    2. the task pattern add task <title> [by YYYY-MM-DD] → Intent("add_task", {"title": …, "due": …}), where due is None when no date was typed;
    3. the keyword table {"report": "daily_report", "today": "daily_report", "summary": "daily_report"} for one-word commands;
    4. otherwise Intent("unknown", {"text": text}).
    

    An alias table maps short names to official routine names: email → email_triage, standup → standup_notes. It lets a person type Log 12 minutes of standup and still produce a valid routine.
    

    The provider is deterministic: the same text always produces the same intent. That property is the reason the OfflineProvider is mandatory and comes first. Tests (pytest, Class 10), the Mid-Term (Part B asks you to read and complete a Tool) and the Final defense must run on any computer, with no network and no key. In Class 10 the ApiProvider becomes a second subclass of Provider with the same parse(text) → Intent method; when the key is missing, the network is down, the free tier answers with HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) status 429 (too many requests) or the reply is not valid JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), JARVIS falls back to the OfflineProvider.
    📽 Slide 28 / 55 — Tools and polymorphism (UML)
    📽 Slide 29 / 55 — Errors never crash the loop
    Tools, polymorphism and errors that never crash the loop
    Tool is an abstract base class (ABC) with a name, a one-line description and an abstract method run(args, store) -> str. Three subclasses implement it today:
    

    • LogTimeTool (log_time) — checks that the routine is one of the six names of the dataset and that the minutes lie between 1 and 480, then stores one entry;
    • AddTaskTool (add_task) — stores a task with an optional due date;
    • DailyReportTool (daily_report) — counts today's entries, today's minutes and the open tasks.
    

    The Agent keeps its tools in a dictionary, {tool.name: tool}, so the intent name finds its tool in one lookup: tool = self.tools.get(intent.name). The line that runs the tool is the same for every subclass:
    

    reply, ok = tool.run(intent.args, self.store), 1
    

    That single call is polymorphism: the object found decides which run() executes, and the Agent never tests the class of the tool. Adding a fourth tool (SummarizeTool, Appendix D) means writing one subclass and one provider rule; Agent.handle() does not change.
    

    Errors. A tool refuses bad input by raising ValueError with a message. The Agent catches only ValueError, turns the message into a reply (could not log_time: minutes must be between 1 and 480, got 0), writes the run with ok = 0 and continues. An intent with no tool gets a polite refusal (sorry, no tool for 'book a flight to Paris') and is also logged. The loop never stops with a traceback in front of the user.
    📽 Slide 31 / 55 — Why offline first · ApiProvider in Class 10
    The Store, the runs table and a fake clock
    The Store owns the database connection and every SQL (Structured Query Language) statement (Appendix D schema). log_run() writes the last step of the loop: the timestamp, the request, the intent, the tool, the provider, ok and the duration in milliseconds (ms). After the six requests of the example, the runs table reads:
    

    📽 Slide 30 / 55 — The runs table: JARVIS's own dataset
    The runs table after the six requests of Example 7.2 (ms column not shown)
    idtsrequestintenttoolproviderok
    12026-11-06T09:00:00log 25 min email_triagelog_timelog_timeoffline1
    22026-11-06T09:01:20Log 12 minutes of standuplog_timelog_timeoffline1
    32026-11-06T09:02:40add task send the invoice reminders by 2026-11-10add_taskadd_taskoffline1
    42026-11-06T09:04:00log 0 min schedulinglog_timelog_timeoffline0
    52026-11-06T09:04:40reportdaily_reportdaily_reportoffline1
    62026-11-06T09:06:00book a flight to ParisunknownNULLoffline0
    

    The runs table is JARVIS's own dataset. In Sprint 2 it gives the requests per day, the share of failed requests (here 2 of 6) and the provider used — numbers that go into the report next to the time saved. Because the request text is stored, requests must never contain personal data: no names, no message contents (Appendix D privacy rule).
    

    The Agent receives its provider, its tools, its store and its clock from outside — dependency injection, met in Class 5. The demo passes a fake clock that moves 40 seconds per call, so its output is identical on every run; the real JARVIS passes datetime.now. The same technique lets a test give the Agent a fake provider or a temporary database.
    

    Key terms of Lesson 7.2
    termmeaning
    agentA program that turns a request in ordinary language into an action through a tool and records each turn.
    requestThe text a person types, e.g. log 25 min email_triage.
    intentThe structured meaning of a request: a name that selects a tool and the arguments it needs.
    providerThe component that converts a request into an intent (OfflineProvider, later ApiProvider).
    toolA small class with a name, a description and run(args, store) -> str that performs one action.
    runs logThe runs table: one row per request (ts, request, intent, tool, provider, ok, ms).
    regular expressionA pattern that describes a set of strings; Python's re module matches it against text.
    named group(?P<name>…): a part of a pattern whose matched text is read with match.group("name").
    quantifierA symbol that sets how many times the previous piece may repeat: +, *, ?, {4}.
    anchor / word boundary^ and $ match the start and the end of the text; \b matches between a word character and a non-word character.
    keyword tableA dictionary that maps one-word commands (report, today) to intent names.
    deterministicAlways producing the same output for the same input; required for tests, the exam and an offline demo.
    polymorphismOne call, tool.run(...), executes the method of whichever subclass the object belongs to.
    abstract base class (ABC)A class with at least one @abstractmethod; it cannot be instantiated and fixes the interface its subclasses implement.
    dependency injectionPassing the parts an object needs (provider, tools, store, clock) from outside instead of creating them inside.

      Step-by-step explanation of the program
      1. Imports and constants. re, sqlite3, time, abc, dataclasses and datetime, all in the standard library. ROUTINES lists the six valid names; ALIASES maps short names to them; SCHEMA holds the three CREATE TABLE statements of Appendix D (reduced).
      2. **FakeClock.** An object that can be called like a function; each call returns a time 40 seconds after the previous one, so the printed timestamps never change between runs.
      3. **Intent.** A frozen dataclass with name and args; default_factory=dict gives each Intent its own dictionary.
      4. **Provider and OfflineProvider.** The ABC (abstract base class) declares parse(). The subclass tries the log pattern, then the task pattern, then the keyword table, and returns unknown when nothing matches; aliases turn standup into standup_notes.
      5. **Tool and its three subclasses.** Each has a name equal to an intent name, a description and run(args, store). LogTimeTool raises ValueError for an unknown routine or minutes outside 1–480.
      6. **Store.** It opens the database (:memory: in the demo), creates the tables, and offers add_entry, add_task, today_summary, log_run and runs. Every INSERT uses ? placeholders and is followed by commit().
      7. **Agent.handle().** Timestamp → provider.parse(text) → dictionary lookup of the tool → tool.run(...) inside try (only ValueError is caught) → store.log_run(...) → reply. An intent without a tool is refused politely and logged with ok = 0.
      8. **main() — tools.** The loop over agent.tools.values() prints three different classes through the same two attributes: polymorphism in its simplest form.
      9. **main() — requests.** The six replies: two logs stored (entries #1 and #2), task #1 with its due date, the refusal of 0 minutes, today: 2 run(s), 37 min logged, 1 open task(s), and sorry, no tool for 'book a flight to Paris'.
      10. **main() — runs table.** Six rows, four with ok=1 and two with ok=0; the unknown request has tool=None (NULL in SQL (Structured Query Language)). The ms column is stored but not printed, because it changes from run to run.
      11. **main() — three phrasings.** The first pattern of the board finds ('30', 'invoice_check') and ('45', 'social_post') but returns None for LOG 20 minutes of scheduling; the OfflineProvider understands all three.
      12. Use the player. Pause when the visualization highlights parse: the Variables panel shows the match object and the captured groups; step on to see the tool, the store call and the new row of the runs table.

      By the end of this part you can…

      📽 Slide 35 / 55 — 7.3 A number is not yet a recommendation
      7.3.1 The recommendation pattern: finding → evidence → decision → risk
      Boréal Studio's owner did not ask for a regression or a runs table. She asked which routine to automate first, how much time it would save and whether a free assistant is good enough. A number becomes useful to her only when it is part of a recommendation. The course uses one pattern with four parts, always in this order:
      

      • Finding — the number that answers her question, with its unit and its direction.
      • Evidence — where the number comes from: the data, the period, the method and the amount of data (n).
      • Decision — what she should do, starting with an action verb, with the expected impact in hours and dollars per month.
      • Risk — what could make the decision wrong, and the mitigation: what the team will do to limit the damage.
      

      The order puts the answer first and the support after it, the principle Barbara Minto taught consultants as the pyramid principle. A text without a decision is a report; without evidence it is an opinion; without a risk it is a sales pitch.
      

      Worked example — the e-mail pilot. From day 10 the assistant triaged e-mail for S1, S2 and S3; S4 and S5 continued by hand. Example 7.3 computes:
      

      📽 Slide 36 / 55 — The e-mail pilot: the difference of the changes
      E-mail triage minutes per run, before and from day 10 (Example 7.3 output)
      groupbefore (days 1–9)nafter (days 10–14)nchange
      pilot S1–S3 (assistant from day 10)35.852713.7315−22.12
      comparison S4–S5 (by hand)34.671834.1010−0.57
      difference of the changes−21.55
      

      The pilot group became 22.12 minutes faster per run. Over the same days the comparison group also changed, by −0.57 minutes, for reasons that have nothing to do with the assistant. The difference of the changes, −22.12 − (−0.57) = −21.55 minutes per run, is the part linked to the assistant (the comparison-group method of Class 4). After the 2-minute review of each assistant-triaged run, the saving is 19.55 minutes per run; at 100 runs a month that is 32.6 hours, or 912 $ per month at 28 $/h. Class 3 used the simple before/after change (20.1 net minutes, 938 $); the comparison group makes the estimate more conservative, and the recommendation reports the conservative number.
      

      📽 Slide 37 / 55 — The recommendation in four parts
      📽 Slide 38 / 55 — Four rules a computer can check
      📽 Slide 39 / 55 — From Lesson 7.1 to a decision: the focus window
      Four rules a computer can check
      A recommendation can be checked for its form before anyone discusses its content. alpha_rehearsal.py applies four rules to a draft:
      

      1. the finding contains at least one digit;
      2. the evidence states the amount of data (n = …);
      3. the decision starts with an action verb (extend, automate, keep, stop, buy, build, start, replace, pilot);
      4. the risk names a mitigation.
      

      The first draft — "JARVIS is faster" / "the pilot" / "We think it is good" / "none" — breaks all four. The rewritten version passes all four:
      

      The e-mail recommendation after rewriting (passes the four rules)
      parttext
      FINDINGAssistant-triaged e-mail took 13.73 min per run against 35.85 min before (−22.12); the comparison group changed by −0.57.
      EVIDENCETeaching dataset, 14 working days, n = 15 pilot runs from 2026-09-25 and n = 10 comparison runs; difference of the changes −21.55 min.
      DECISIONExtend assistant triage to all five staff for a four-week trial: about 32.6 h and 912 $ saved per month after the 2-minute review.
      RISKOnly 15 pilot runs by three people. Mitigation: keep the review of each run, measure again after four weeks, stop if an urgent e-mail is mis-sorted.
      

      The same pattern turns Lesson 7.1 into a decision:
      

      • Finding. Each extra interruption is associated with about 2.2 more minutes per stand-up run (r = 0.88, R² = 0.78).
      • Evidence. 70 manual runs, 14 working days, 5 staff, teaching dataset; slope checked against statistics.linear_regression.
      • Decision. Pilot a 15-minute focus window (notifications muted 9:00–9:15) for two weeks, then measure again.
      • Risk. An association, not a proven cause; busy days bring both interruptions and longer notes. Mitigation: compare the two weeks with the two weeks before, and with one person who keeps notifications on.
      

      Notice the verb: pilot, not adopt. Weak or causal-sounding evidence calls for a reversible decision.

      7.3.2 Presenting an Alpha in five minutes
      An alpha is the first version of a product that runs from start to finish on real data with its core logic in place, shown to get feedback — not a finished product. The repository tags mark the path: alpha-0.3 today, beta-0.1 in Class 10, rc-1.0 on December 18 (release candidate), v1.0-final for the defense.
      

      Each team has five minutes, followed by three minutes of feedback. The run of show — the planned sequence of segments with their durations — is the same for every team:
      

      📽 Slide 41 / 55 — The five-minute run of show
      The five-minute run of show and the rehearsal of Example 7.3
      segmentwhat it containsplanned (s)measured (s)difference
      problemThe owner's question in one sentence3035+5
      design (UML (Unified Modeling Language))The classes and the agent loop on one slide6080+20
      live demoOne request logged, one report printed — offline120150+30
      first numbersr, b and a; the e-mail finding6055−5
      next stepsWhat Brick 9 and Class 10 add3025−5
      totalslot: 300 s300345+45
      

      One message should run through the five segments: what JARVIS already does and the first number that matters to the owner. Chris Anderson's TED (Technology, Entertainment, Design) talk of this lesson makes the same point for any talk: one central idea, built step by step.
      

      Demo hygiene — the habits that keep a live demo short and safe:
      

      • run the exact commands the morning of the demo, in a fresh terminal, from a fresh clone if possible;
      • keep fallback screenshots (or a short screen recording) on a second device;
      • one person types, one person talks;
      • enlarge the terminal font (20 points or more) and close notifications and other windows;
      • use the offline mode: the demo must not depend on the room's Wi-Fi;
      • rehearse with a stopwatch and trim the segment that overruns most.
      

      In the rehearsal of Example 7.3 the team measures 35, 80, 150, 55 and 25 seconds: 345 seconds, 45 over the slot. The program ranks the overruns — live demo +30, design +20, problem +5 — so the team cuts the live demo first, for example by opening the terminal and the dataset before the presentation starts.
      

      When something goes wrong. If the demo crashes: say what happened in one sentence, switch to the screenshots, continue the run of show, and write the bug down for the fix-it sprint. If the projector fails: talk through the printed UML and the numbers. If someone asks a question you cannot answer: "Good question — we will check and add the answer to the report."
      

      📽 Slide 42 / 55 — Rehearsal: 345 s against a 300 s slot
      📽 Slide 45 / 55 — 2 stars + 1 wish
      7.3.3 Giving and receiving feedback: 2 stars + 1 wish
      After each demo, a peer team writes a feedback slip with two stars and one wish. A star is a specific strength; a wish is one specific improvement. Three properties make a comment useful:
      

      • specific — it names an artefact (a slide, a command, a chart, a number) and an observable fact: "Label the axes of the scatter plot with their units";
      • about the work, not the person — "the results slide has no sources", never "you are disorganised";
      • actionable — the team can act on it before Thursday 23:59.
      

      Vague phrases such as "good job" or "make it better" carry no information a team can use. The answer to a vague comment is a follow-up question: "Which part should we change first?" LeeAnn Renninger's TED (Technology, Entertainment, Design) talk calls the specific part a data point: an observation anyone in the room could confirm.
      

      Receiving feedback follows four steps: listen without defending, say thank you, write every comment down, ask one clarifying question when a comment is vague. Afterwards the team sorts the wishes by theme and keeps the top three actions in docs/feedback_log.md — a Brick 7 deliverable. In Example 7.3, five slips give two wishes about charts, one about evidence and one about timing, plus two vague comments that need a follow-up question:
      

      docs/feedback_log.md produced by Example 7.3
      rankthemewishes behind it (source)
      1chartsLabel the axes of the scatter plot with their units (Team Nord); Draw the regression line on the scatter plot, not only the value of r (Team Pont)
      2evidenceSay how many runs each average comes from when you show it (Team Rive)
      3timingOpen the terminal before you start so the demo stays under two minutes (instructor)
      follow-upvagueTeam Lac star "Good job"; Team Lac wish "Make it better"
      

      The instructor's notes during the demos use two dimensions of the course rubric (Appendix B): Communication (clear structure, timing, answers) and Tech Implementation (a working loop, OOP (object-oriented programming) quality, the offline fallback). The same rubric returns for peer review in Sprint 3, the dress rehearsal (Class 14) and the Final.

      findingThe number that answers the owner's question, with its unit and direction.
      evidenceThe source, period, method and amount of data (n) behind the finding.
      decisionWhat the owner should do, starting with an action verb, with the expected impact.
      risk / mitigationWhat could make the decision wrong / what the team will do to limit that damage.
      difference of the changesThe change of the pilot group minus the change of the comparison group over the same period.
      comparison groupUnits that did not receive the change (here S4 and S5), used to estimate what would have happened anyway.
      alphaThe first version that runs end to end on real data with its core logic, shown to get feedback.
      run of showThe planned sequence of presentation segments with their durations (here 300 seconds).
      demo hygieneThe habits that keep a live demo short and safe: rehearsed commands, fallback, one typist, large font, offline mode.
      fallbackA prepared alternative (screenshots, recording) used when the live demo fails.
      starA specific strength of the work, named with an artefact and an observable fact.
      wishOne specific, actionable improvement.
      feedback logdocs/feedback_log.md: the top-3 actions chosen from the feedback, with their sources.

      Alpha rehearsal on Thursday evening
      Task of the exampleConvert the e-mail pilot numbers into a four-part recommendation that passes four rules, check the measured run of show against the 300-second slot, and turn five feedback slips into the top-3 actions of docs/feedback_log.md.How it relates to Lesson 7.3It applies the three parts of Lesson 7.3 — recommendation pattern, five-minute Alpha with demo hygiene, 2 stars + 1 wish — to the team's own Alpha.
      Thursday, November 5, 2026, the evening before the Alpha demo. The team meets for a last rehearsal. It has three questions to settle before going home: is our recommendation sentence complete, do we fit in five minutes, and which three comments from the practice round do we act on first?
      

      The team writes a small program instead of arguing: it computes the pilot numbers from the dataset, rejects the hurried draft, prints the corrected four parts, compares the stopwatch times with the plan, and sorts the feedback slips of four peer teams and the instructor.

      Program 7.3 — runs in the page
      Program 7.3 — alpha_rehearsal.py
      Task of the programCompute the e-mail pilot effect, reject an incomplete recommendation and accept the four-part version, compare the rehearsal times with the 300-second plan, and sort feedback slips into top-3 actions.How it relates to Lesson 7.3It produces the recommendation and the feedback log that Brick 7 asks for; the visualization fills the recommendation card, the run-of-show bars and the feedback board while it runs.
      Every line of code is preceded by a comment line that says what the line does and why. The player replays a recorded execution of the real program (Python 3.12+, standard library only) step by step; its console is identical to the output of python code/alpha_rehearsal.py.
      Execution steps (every executed step stays here)
        Variables at this step (yellow = changed)
        Console output
        Visualization of the lesson concept
        Step-by-step explanation of the program
        1. Constants. The given values of the course (28 $/h, 100 runs a month, 2 review minutes), the pilot start date and staff, and the action verbs a decision may start with.
        2. **email_groups().** It reads the dataset and puts the minutes of every e-mail run into one of four lists: pilot or comparison, before or after 2026-09-25. ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 8601 dates compare correctly as text.
        3. **Recommendation.** A dataclass with four text fields and a method problems() that applies the four rules and returns the list of violations.
        4. **PLAN, REHEARSAL, SLOT.** The five planned segments with seconds and speaker, the stopwatch times and the 300-second slot.
        5. **SLIPS, VAGUE, THEMES.** Five feedback slips, the vague phrases to detect and the keyword table that sorts a wish into a theme.
        6. **is_specific() and theme_of().** A comment is specific when it has at least six words and no vague phrase; the theme is the first keyword found, or other.
        7. Check 1. The four means (35.85 → 13.73 and 34.67 → 34.10), the changes −22.12 and −0.57, the difference −21.55, the net saving 19.55 minutes and the impact 32.6 h and 912 $ per month; the draft fails four rules, the final version none, and its four parts are printed.
        8. Check 2. A loop over the plan prints planned and measured seconds, the difference and the running total: 345 seconds against 300, so +45; the overruns are sorted to show what to trim first.
        9. Check 3. Each star and each wish is tested; vague ones go to a follow-up list, specific wishes to their theme. The themes are ranked by the number of wishes and the program prints the Markdown text of docs/feedback_log.md.
        10. Use the player. Pause during Check 1 to see the draft's problems appear in the recommendation card; during Check 2 the bars grow segment by segment; during Check 3 the board counts the themes.

        Formative quiz — Lesson 7.3
        Formative, not summative. This quiz is for practice only: it is not graded and does not count toward your final grade. Four multiple-choice questions (one answer, 4 options) and two multiple-select questions (6 options; the number of right answers is given in round brackets). Academic integrity — Legal Notice §18.
        Question 1. Which sentence is the decision of the e-mail recommendation?MCQ (multiple-choice question)
        Hint: A decision tells the owner what to do and starts with an action verb.
        Question 2. A rehearsal measures 35, 80, 150, 55 and 25 seconds against the plan 30, 60, 120, 60, 30. Which segment should the team trim first?MCQ (multiple-choice question)
        Hint: Compute measured minus planned for each segment.
        Question 3. During the Alpha demo the program stops with a traceback. What is the best reaction?MCQ (multiple-choice question)
        Hint: The slot is five minutes and the rest of the run of show still has value.
        Question 4. Which comment is a usable wish?MCQ (multiple-choice question)
        Hint: Could the team act on it tonight, knowing exactly what to change?
        Question 5. Which elements belong in the evidence part of a recommendation?MSQ (multiple-select question) (select 3) (3 correct answers expected)
        Hint: Evidence lets someone else check where the number comes from.
        Question 6. Which two actions belong to receiving feedback in this course?MSQ (multiple-select question) (select 2) (2 correct answers expected)
        Hint: Listen, thank, write down, clarify — then choose.

        Key terms and abbreviations of Class 7
        lessontermmeaning
        7.1explanatory variable (x)The variable used to explain or predict another one; here, interruptions per run.
        7.1response variable (y)The variable we want to explain or predict; here, minutes per run.
        7.1deviationThe distance of a value from its mean, x − x̄; negative below the mean, positive above it.
        7.1Sxx, Syy, SxyThe sums of squared deviations of x and of y, and the sum of cross-products of the deviations.
        7.1Pearson correlation coefficient (r)Sxy / √(Sxx·Syy), between −1 and +1: strength and direction of a straight-line relationship.
        7.1simple linear regressionA model ŷ = a + b·x with one explanatory variable, fitted by least squares.
        7.1slope (b)Sxy / Sxx: the change in predicted y for one more unit of x (minutes per interruption).
        7.1intercept (a)ȳ − b·x̄: the predicted y when x = 0; meaningful only when x = 0 is inside the data.
        7.1fitted value (ŷ)The point of the line above a given x.
        7.1residual (e)y − ŷ, the observed minus the fitted value.
        7.1least squaresThe method that chooses a and b so that the sum of squared residuals (SSE (sum of squared errors)) is as small as possible.
        7.1coefficient of determination (R²)1 − SSE/SST (total sum of squares) = r² for one explanatory variable: the share of the variation of y that the line accounts for.
        7.1interpolation / extrapolationA forecast inside / outside the range of x values that were observed.
        7.1confounding variableA third variable that influences both x and y and can create a correlation without a direct cause.
        7.1oracleA trusted implementation (here the statistics module) used only to check your own code.
        7.2agentA program that turns a request in ordinary language into an action through a tool and records each turn.
        7.2requestThe text a person types, e.g. log 25 min email_triage.
        7.2intentThe structured meaning of a request: a name that selects a tool and the arguments it needs.
        7.2providerThe component that converts a request into an intent (OfflineProvider, later ApiProvider).
        7.2toolA small class with a name, a description and run(args, store) -> str that performs one action.
        7.2runs logThe runs table: one row per request (ts, request, intent, tool, provider, ok, ms).
        7.2regular expressionA pattern that describes a set of strings; Python's re module matches it against text.
        7.2named group(?P<name>…): a part of a pattern whose matched text is read with match.group("name").
        7.2quantifierA symbol that sets how many times the previous piece may repeat: +, *, ?, {4}.
        7.2anchor / word boundary^ and $ match the start and the end of the text; \b matches between a word character and a non-word character.
        7.2keyword tableA dictionary that maps one-word commands (report, today) to intent names.
        7.2deterministicAlways producing the same output for the same input; required for tests, the exam and an offline demo.
        7.2polymorphismOne call, tool.run(...), executes the method of whichever subclass the object belongs to.
        7.2abstract base class (ABC)A class with at least one @abstractmethod; it cannot be instantiated and fixes the interface its subclasses implement.
        7.2dependency injectionPassing the parts an object needs (provider, tools, store, clock) from outside instead of creating them inside.
        7.3recommendationA statement in four parts — finding, evidence, decision, risk — that tells the owner what to do and why.
        7.3findingThe number that answers the owner's question, with its unit and direction.
        7.3evidenceThe source, period, method and amount of data (n) behind the finding.
        7.3decisionWhat the owner should do, starting with an action verb, with the expected impact.
        7.3risk / mitigationWhat could make the decision wrong / what the team will do to limit that damage.
        7.3difference of the changesThe change of the pilot group minus the change of the comparison group over the same period.
        7.3comparison groupUnits that did not receive the change (here S4 and S5), used to estimate what would have happened anyway.
        7.3alphaThe first version that runs end to end on real data with its core logic, shown to get feedback.
        7.3run of showThe planned sequence of presentation segments with their durations (here 300 seconds).
        7.3demo hygieneThe habits that keep a live demo short and safe: rehearsed commands, fallback, one typist, large font, offline mode.
        7.3fallbackA prepared alternative (screenshots, recording) used when the live demo fails.
        7.3starA specific strength of the work, named with an artefact and an observable fact.
        7.3wishOne specific, actionable improvement.
        7.3feedback logdocs/feedback_log.md: the top-3 actions chosen from the feedback, with their sources.
